128 years ago today, an American commodore sailed into a fortified enemy harbor before dawn, told his flag captain “You may fire when ready, Gridley,” and in six hours destroyed an entire fleet without losing a single man.

The Battle of Manila Bay is the most lopsided naval victory in modern history, and almost no one remembers it.

When the Spanish-American War broke out in late April 1898, George Dewey was a 60-year-old commodore commanding the Asiatic Squadron out of Hong Kong. He had six warships, no nearby base, and orders from a then-obscure Assistant Secretary of the Navy named Theodore Roosevelt to attack the Spanish fleet in the Philippines the moment war was declared. The British, neutral, told him he had to leave Hong Kong. Dewey sailed for Manila on April 27 with what he had.

The Spanish admiral Patricio Montojo had ten warships waiting, plus the shore batteries of Manila and the guns at Corregidor. On paper it was a fair fight. In reality it was not. Most of Montojo’s ships were wooden, undergunned, and barely seaworthy. He knew it. Rather than fight at the harbor mouth where his shore guns could help, he anchored his fleet off Cavite in shallow water, reportedly so his sailors would have a shorter swim when their ships were sunk.

Dewey arrived off the entrance to Manila Bay on the night of April 30. The accepted wisdom was that the channel was mined and the forts at Corregidor would shred any fleet that tried to enter at night. Dewey ran the channel anyway, in the dark, in single file, lights doused. The Spanish gunners at El Fraile fired three shots. The Americans fired back twice and kept going. By dawn on May 1, the entire squadron was inside the bay and bearing down on Cavite.

At 5:41 AM, Dewey turned to Charles Gridley, captain of the flagship Olympia, and said the line that made him famous: “You may fire when ready, Gridley.” The Olympia’s forward 8-inch gun opened up. The other five ships followed.

Dewey ran his squadron in a long oval, firing a broadside on each pass. Five times he made the loop. Around 7:30 AM, he broke off to take stock. The story later told was that he stopped for breakfast. He probably stopped because he thought he was out of shells. He wasn’t.

By the time he resumed at 11:16 AM, the Spanish fleet was finished. The flagship Reina Cristina had been hit repeatedly trying to charge the Olympia and was burning. The Castilla, a wooden cruiser whose engines didn’t work, had been towed into position and was now an inferno. One by one the Spanish ships struck their colors, were scuttled by their crews, or burned to the waterline. By 12:30 PM, every Spanish warship in Manila Bay was destroyed or surrendered.

The final tally is almost hard to believe. Spanish dead: 161. Ten warships lost. American dead: zero. American wounded: nine. One sailor died of heatstroke in the engine room. That was the only loss.

The political consequences were enormous and almost entirely unintended. Dewey held Manila Bay but had no troops to take the city. He sat at anchor for three months waiting for the Army. When American troops finally landed and Manila fell in August, the United States suddenly owned the Philippines, an archipelago that no one in Washington had been thinking about three months earlier.

The country that had spent a century defining itself against European colonialism had, in one morning off Cavite, become a Pacific empire. The occupation triggered the Philippine-American War, which killed more Americans than the entire Spanish-American War did and hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. The Philippines would not be independent until 1946.

Dewey came home a national hero, promoted to Admiral of the Navy, the only officer ever to hold that rank. Today he is largely forgotten.

But on this morning in 1898, before most of Manila had finished breakfast, a 60-year-old commodore turned the United States into a world power in six hours and never lost a man.

.@stripe just launched @link's agent wallet on April 29 at sessions 2026 in San Francisco. here's a proper breakdown of what it means for agentic commerce:

link is stripe's consumer wallet with roughly 250 million users globally. it stores cards, bank accounts, and increasingly stablecoins, with recent integrations including usdc payouts to meta creators in colombia and the philippines.

the new agent wallet lets a user grant an ai agent permission to transact on their behalf. authorization runs through an oauth flow: the user authorizes the agent, the agent creates a spend request with full purchase context, and the user approves before any payment credential reaches the agent.

the underlying infrastructure runs on a separate stripe product called issuing for agents, which provisions virtual cards that agents use to make purchases on the user's behalf.

initial support covers cards and shared payment tokens, with stablecoin and agentic token support promised to be coming soon.

stripe paired the launch with a universal commerce protocol (UCP) partnership with google for selling inside ai mode and gemini, and an agentic commerce suite that connects wix, bigcommerce, and woocommerce merchants into ai shopping surfaces through one integration.

profile_bio.description: the control layer for agent economies.
